title: Distributed locks, leader election, ZooKeeper/etcd, fencing tokens
scopeHtml: Scope: Lease locks, paused-holder problem, fencing tokens, Redis/Redlock, ZooKeeper and etcd recipes, leader election, DB locks. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why distributed locks exist
notes.html:
A distributed lock lets only one process across many machines do a job at a time. Examples: only one worker runs the nightly billing job, only one node renews a shared cache, only one writer updates a file in object storage.

First ask whether you need a lock at all. Cheaper alternatives:

  • Database constraint or row lock: UPDATE ... WHERE status='NEW' or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
  • Idempotency: make doing the job twice harmless.
  • Single consumer per partition: Kafka gives one consumer per partition in a group.
  • Optimistic concurrency: version column, compare-and-set.

Two reasons to lock (Martin Kleppmann's framing):

  1. Efficiency: avoid doing duplicate work. If the lock fails occasionally, you just waste some CPU. A simple Redis lock is fine.
  2. Correctness: two holders corrupt data. Then you need a lock with fencing, built on consensus.

Worked example. 20 pods each run a cron at 02:00 to send daily emails to 1M users. Without a lock: 20x duplicate emails. With a lock (or a leader): one pod does the job in about 10 minutes. With idempotent INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING per (user, date), duplicates are harmless and you may need no lock.

Industry examples. Kubernetes controllers use a lease object in etcd for leader election; Spring Batch and Quartz use DB locks; Uber's Cadence/Temporal use consensus-backed storage to ensure one workflow owner.

Everyday analogy. One key to a shared meeting room: whoever holds the key can use it, everyone else waits.

Common interview traps.

  • Reaching for a distributed lock when a unique constraint would do.
  • Not saying whether the lock is for efficiency or correctness.

notes.title: Lease-based locks, TTLs and the paused-process problem
notes.html:
A lock must expire, or a crashed holder blocks everyone forever. So distributed locks are leases: a lock with a time limit (TTL).

Flow: acquire with TTL 30 s, do work, extend (heartbeat) every 10 s, release when done. If the holder dies, the lock vanishes after at most 30 s.

The nasty problem: the holder cannot know that its lease expired. A long GC pause, VM freeze, slow disk or network stall can stop it for longer than the TTL. When it wakes up it still believes it holds the lock and writes to the resource, while a second holder already took over.

t=0    A acquires lock (TTL 30s)
t=5    A starts a long GC pause (45 s)
t=30   lock expires
t=31   B acquires lock, writes to storage
t=50   A wakes up, still thinks it holds the lock, writes to storage  <-- CORRUPTION

The lock service cannot fix this; the resource must defend itself (fencing tokens, next section).

Real incident pattern. Intermittent duplicated or overwritten records only under load or during GC storms. Metric: GC pause duration p99 near or above the lease TTL; lock "lost" log lines appear after the damage.

Decision gravity. TTL choice: short means fast failover but more false expiries during pauses; long means slow recovery. Common: TTL 10 to 30 s, renew at one third of TTL. Reversible config, but the correctness model (fencing or not) is a one-way design decision.

Industry examples. Chubby (Google) popularised coarse-grained leases; DynamoDB lock client and Kubernetes Lease objects use TTL leases. Kubernetes defaults for leader election: lease duration 15 s, renew deadline 10 s, retry period 2 s (confirm in the client-go docs for your version).

Everyday analogy. A hotel keycard that stops working at noon: if you fell asleep in the room past noon, housekeeping enters; you still think the room is yours.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "I checked I hold the lock just before writing" is safe. The pause can happen after the check.
  • Using wall-clock time to decide lease validity (clock jumps). Use monotonic time with a safety margin.

notes.title: Fencing tokens
notes.html:
A fencing token is a number that increases every time the lock is granted. The protected resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any request carrying a lower one.

This solves the paused-holder problem: the stale holder's write carries an old token and is refused.

A acquires lock -> token 33
A pauses
lock expires; B acquires -> token 34
B writes with token 34   -> storage records max=34, OK
A wakes, writes token 33 -> storage: 33 < 34, REJECT

Requirements:

  • The lock service issues strictly increasing tokens (ZooKeeper zxid/node version, etcd revision, or a counter in a consensus store).
  • The resource must check tokens. That means the database, storage or downstream API has to participate (e.g. a column fence BIGINT with UPDATE ... WHERE fence <= :token). If the resource cannot, fencing is impossible and you need to use the resource's own atomic compare-and-set instead.
-- Storage-side fencing check, atomic
UPDATE jobs
SET payload = :p, fence = :token
WHERE id = :id AND fence <= :token;   -- 0 rows updated => stale holder, abort

Industry examples. HDFS NameNode HA fences the old active namenode (including storage-level fencing with shared edit logs). Kafka uses producer epochs and leader epochs as fencing tokens. Raft terms play the same role.

Decision gravity. Fencing is a design-level choice: adopt it when correctness matters. Alternative STONITH-style fencing powers off the node (heavy, used in HA clusters). Retrofitting token checks into a resource later is hard, so decide early.

Everyday analogy. Numbered tickets at a ticket window: the clerk only serves a ticket with a number at least as high as the last served; an old ticket is turned away.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the lock prevents two writers". With pauses it does not, without fencing.
  • Putting the token check in the client rather than the storage.
  • Using random UUIDs as tokens; they must be monotonic.

notes.title: Redis locks and Redlock
notes.html:
Simple Redis lock: SET lock:billing <random-id> NX PX 30000. NX means set only if absent; PX is the TTL in ms. Release with a Lua script that deletes only if the value still equals your random id (so you never delete someone else's lock).

# acquire
redis-cli SET lock:billing 7f3a-uuid NX PX 30000
# release (atomic compare-and-delete)
redis-cli EVAL "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 lock:billing 7f3a-uuid

Problems:

  • Single Redis master fails over asynchronously: the lock write may not have reached the replica, so a promoted replica lets a second client acquire. Two holders.
  • No built-in fencing token.
  • TTL pause problem as above.

Redlock (antirez's proposal) acquires the lock on a majority of N=5 independent Redis masters within a small time bound. Kleppmann's critique: it depends on bounded clocks and delays and gives no fencing token, so it is unsafe for correctness, though fine for efficiency. Antirez disputed parts of this. Interview-safe position: Redis locks are acceptable for efficiency; for correctness use a consensus-based system with fencing.

Worked example. Rate: a single Redis does about 100,000 SET ops/s, so lock throughput is rarely the limit. 1,000 pods contending for one lock every 30 s is trivial load.

Industry examples. Redisson (Java) and redis-py implement lock helpers; Shopify and many companies use Redis locks for de-duplication of jobs.

Decision gravity. Starting with a Redis lock is cheap and reversible, provided the protected action is idempotent. Moving to a consensus lock later is a modest change if you kept the lock behind an interface.

Everyday analogy. A sign on a door written in pencil: quick, but if the sign-keeper loses their notebook another person may write a second sign.

Common interview traps.

  • Releasing with a plain DEL (can delete another client's lock).
  • Using SETNX then EXPIRE as two commands (crash between them leaves a permanent lock). Use one atomic SET NX PX.
  • Calling Redlock "provably safe".

notes.title: ZooKeeper and etcd as coordination services
notes.html:
ZooKeeper and etcd are small, strongly consistent, replicated stores built on consensus (ZAB and Raft). They are designed for locks, leader election, configuration and service discovery, not for bulk data.

ZooKeeper primitives:

  • znodes in a tree; ephemeral znodes vanish when the client session ends (session timeout, say 10 s); sequential znodes get an increasing suffix; watches notify clients of changes.
  • Lock recipe: create ephemeral+sequential /lock/node-000000042. List children; if yours has the lowest number you hold the lock; otherwise watch only the node just before yours (avoids a thundering herd on release). The sequence number or zxid can act as a fencing token.

etcd primitives:

  • Key-value with a global revision (monotonic), leases with TTL (keys attached to a lease disappear when it expires), transactions (compare-and-swap), and watch streams.
  • Lock recipe: create key /lock/billing/<leaseID> with the lease, the holder with the lowest creation revision wins; the revision is the fencing token. The concurrency package in Go provides Mutex and Election.

Typical limits. etcd values are meant to be small (default request limit about 1.5 MiB, DB quota default 2 GB; confirm per version). ZooKeeper znode data limit is about 1 MB by default and it keeps all data in memory. A 3 or 5 node ensemble handles roughly thousands to tens of thousands of writes/s; reads scale with followers.

Industry examples. Kubernetes stores all state in etcd; Kafka (older versions) used ZooKeeper for controller election and metadata (now KRaft); HBase, Hadoop HA and Solr use ZooKeeper; Consul offers sessions and KV locks on Raft.

Decision gravity. Choosing a managed coordination service is a deliberate dependency: operationally heavy but battle-tested. Alternative: lease row in your existing Postgres (simple, one fewer system, but not designed for high churn). Moving between them is moderately reversible if hidden behind a leader-election interface.

Everyday analogy. A notary office: small, slow, extremely careful records that everyone trusts, as opposed to a fast but forgetful notice board.

Common interview traps.

  • Using ZooKeeper/etcd as a general database or queue.
  • Forgetting session timeout vs lease TTL: a client that stalls loses ephemeral nodes.
  • Having every waiter watch the same node (thundering herd).

notes.title: Leader election
notes.html:
Leader election picks one node among many to act as the coordinator or sole writer, and picks a new one if it fails. It is the same problem as a distributed lock held for a long time.

Approaches:

  1. Built into the data system: Raft/Paxos groups (etcd, Kafka KRaft, CockroachDB ranges) elect leaders internally.
  2. Lock-based: all candidates try to create the same lease key; the winner is leader and keeps renewing. If it stops renewing, others compete again (Kubernetes controller manager, scheduler).
  3. Database row: UPDATE leader SET owner=:me, expires=now()+30s WHERE expires < now() OR owner=:me. Simple, with the caveats of clocks and fencing.
  4. Bully / ring algorithms: textbook, rarely used in production.
# Kubernetes leader election flags for controllers (typical values)
leaderElection:
  leaderElect: true
  leaseDuration: 15s
  renewDeadline: 10s
  retryPeriod: 2s

Failover time is about the lease duration plus retry period: here 15 to 17 s. Shorter means faster failover but more flapping on a GC pause or API server slowness.

Worked example. 3 replicas of a scheduler pod, leader dies at t=0. Lease (15 s) expires at t=15 s, standby tries at its next retry (within 2 s) and wins by t=17 s. Scheduling stalls for about 17 s but no duplicate scheduling occurs.

What the old leader must do. Stop acting the moment it fails to renew (step down quickly: renewDeadline < leaseDuration) and also be protected by fencing at the resource.

Industry examples. Kafka partition leaders (ISR-based, with leader epochs), HDFS active/standby namenodes with ZKFC, Elasticsearch master election, Kubernetes components via Lease objects.

Decision gravity. Single leader is simple and high throughput but has failover pauses and a ceiling at one node's capacity. Alternatives: partition work so each partition has its own leader (sharding), or leaderless designs with conflict resolution. Moving between them is a major architecture change.

Everyday analogy. A relay baton: whoever holds it is in charge, and if the runner collapses, the team picks the next runner after a short pause.

Common interview traps.

  • Not handling the old leader still running (zombie leader).
  • Having failover time shorter than the longest realistic GC or network pause.
  • Believing a leader election makes the leader's side effects safe without fencing.

notes.title: Database-based locks and advisory locks
notes.html:
Sometimes the lock service you already have, a relational DB, is the right tool. Options in Postgres:

  • Row lock: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a row; released at commit/rollback. A crashed connection releases automatically.
  • Advisory locks: pg_advisory_lock(key) (session scoped) or pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) (transaction scoped); locks are on application-chosen numbers, not rows. pg_try_advisory_lock does not block.
  • Queue pattern: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10 lets many workers pull different jobs safely.
-- Only one worker runs the job; others skip immediately
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42);   -- returns true for one session only
-- ... do work ...
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42);

-- Job queue pattern
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'NEW'
ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Why it works well: the lock is tied to the connection or transaction; if the process dies the DB frees it, with no TTL guessing. Caveats: ties up a connection per lock; works only if everyone talks to the same primary (not across replicas or regions); session-level advisory locks leak through connection poolers like PgBouncer in transaction mode (use transaction-level locks there).

Worked example. 50 workers, a jobs table. SKIP LOCKED lets each take a 10-row batch with no blocking; throughput of several thousand jobs/s on one Postgres is realistic.

Industry examples. Que, GoodJob, River and Oban (queue libraries) use Postgres SKIP LOCKED/advisory locks; Rails' with_advisory_lock gems; Flyway/Liquibase use a lock to serialise migrations.

Decision gravity. Easy, reversible, but it ties availability of the lock to your primary database and adds load there. Good until the lock contention itself becomes a hot spot.

Everyday analogy. A shared whiteboard marker held by whoever is at the board; if they walk out of the building, security takes it back automatically.

Common interview traps.

  • Session advisory locks behind a transaction-mode pooler.
  • Holding a row lock across a slow external call (blocks others, long transactions bloat the DB).

notes.title: Common failure scenarios and a decision guide
notes.html:
Scenarios to reason through in an interview:

Failure What happens Defence
Holder crashes Lease expires, others proceed TTL / session / DB frees lock
Holder paused (GC, VM) Two believe they hold the lock Fencing token checked by resource
Network partition Holder cannot renew Holder steps down at renewDeadline
Lock service loses quorum No one can acquire Fail closed (stop the job) or degrade deliberately
Clock jump Lease length misjudged Monotonic clocks, safety margin
Lock service failover (Redis) Lock lost Use consensus store when correctness matters

Heuristics:

  • Idempotency beats locks. If the job can be repeated safely, a lock only saves cost.
  • Keep critical sections short and never hold a lock over a remote call you cannot bound.
  • Fail closed if you cannot confirm the lock: stop and retry rather than proceed.
  • Add a timeout to acquiring too, with jitter on retries.

Everyday analogy. Booking the only meeting room: the booking system is useful, but you also lock the door from inside so a late-arriving group cannot walk in on stale information.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing the happy path only. The interviewer asks "what if the holder freezes for 60 seconds?"
  • Choosing a lock service with no discussion of its failure mode.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• First try to avoid locks: unique constraints, idempotency, single consumer per partition, optimistic CAS.
  • Distributed locks are leases with TTLs; a paused holder cannot know it lost the lease.
  • Fencing tokens (monotonic numbers checked by the resource) make locks safe for correctness; Raft terms, Kafka epochs and etcd revisions are the same idea.
  • Redis SET NX PX plus a safe unlock script is fine for efficiency; Redlock is debated and gives no fencing.
  • ZooKeeper (ephemeral+sequential znodes, watch predecessor) and etcd (leases, revisions, txn) are consensus-backed coordination services; keep data small.
  • Leader election = long-held lock; failover time is about lease duration plus retry period; the old leader must step down and be fenced.
  • Postgres advisory locks and SKIP LOCKED are excellent for simple cases; beware poolers and long transactions.
